text: 18. Current Project Status

This section is the honest, code-grounded status report for CoLab as it stands today. It is written to be the single source of truth for the next five years, so it deliberately separates what is *shipped and verified* from what *works but is incomplete*, from what is *not built at all*, and from the *technical debt, known issues, and production risks* that an operator or engineer inheriting this system must understand before they touch it. Every claim here was checked against the real repository state — the 47 ordered migrations under `database/migrations/`, the Express routes under `backend/app/src/`, the Next.js components under `frontend/app/src/`, and the deployment compose files at the repo root — not against marketing copy or aspiration. Where the codebase contradicts a previously-stated assumption (for example the session-token lifetime, or whether the AI assistant has a UI), this section corrects it.

**Plain-language summary.** CoLab is a working, enterprise-styled team-collaboration application: people sign up, log in, chat in DMs / groups / channels with rich text, voice notes, reactions, threads, files and read receipts; they place 1:1 and group calls and schedule full video meetings over LiveKit; they manage tasks, reminders, contacts, a calendar and a notifications feed; and they do all of this through one polished single-page front end with six themes and deep accessibility/responsiveness controls. The pieces that are *not* finished are clearly fenced off: AI is wired but mostly hidden, the agent system is an empty scaffold, the MCP server is a standalone prototype, server-side recording needs infrastructure that is not provisioned, and end-to-end encryption is a real but Phase-1 (DM-only, no forward secrecy) feature that ships turned **off**.

title: How to read the maturity labels
text: DONE = built and exercised (most are live-verified; calls/meetings media is code-complete but only fully verifiable on an HTTPS+TURN deployment). PARTIAL = the code path exists and runs but the feature is incomplete, hidden behind a default-off flag, or depends on infrastructure that is not turned on. ABSENT = there is no functioning implementation, only a scaffold or a static UI placeholder.

title: What is actually running, at a glance

text: 18.1 Completed — Shipped and Verified

The following capabilities are fully implemented end-to-end: a frontend surface, a backend route + service, a database table (or an explicit reason there is none), and realtime wiring where applicable. These are the load-bearing features of the product and they are exercised in normal use. The one honest caveat that applies across calls and meetings is the **media plane**: the application logic, signalling, token-minting and host controls are complete and verified, but cross-network media delivery can only be fully proven on a deployment that has HTTPS (a secure context is mandatory for `getUserMedia`) and a reachable TURN relay — see the Production Risks subsection (18.6).

18.1.2 Authentication and session — verified behavior

Auth is complete and enforced server-side. Passwords are hashed with Node's built-in `scrypt` and stored as `saltHex:hashHex` (16-byte salt, 64-byte key); verification is constant-time via `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. The signup credential policy (`credentialPolicy.ts`) is the authority — it validates email shape, rejects ~70 disposable-email providers, and enforces a 9-character minimum password with lower+upper+digit+special and a ~60-entry common-password blocklist. The frontend `passwordPolicy.ts` is a non-authoritative UX mirror only. Every auth event (signup/login/logout/account-delete) is written to the append-only `audit_log`.

title: Correction: session JWT lives 7 days, not 1 hour
text: The API session JWT is HS256 with payload {sub, name} and a default TTL of **7d** (env AUTH_TOKEN_TTL, config/src/index.ts line 19) — verified against the source. The ~1h / 3600s lifetime that is sometimes attributed to 'the token' actually belongs to the SEPARATE short-lived LiveKit room token (LIVEKIT_TOKEN_TTL_SEC, default 3600). There is NO refresh-token or silent-remint flow: a single long-lived access JWT is issued at login and the user re-authenticates on expiry. Revocation is handled by a token blocklist (Redis-backed, in-memory fallback) keyed by the token's signature segment with TTL = token exp.
18.1.3 Messaging depth — what is actually shipped

Messaging is the most mature subsystem. The single `conversations` / `conversation_members` / `messages` schema serves DMs (`kind='dm'`/`'self'`), groups (`'group'`) and channels (`'channel'`) with the same code path — there is no separate channel or group table, only a discriminating `kind` column. Messages are stored as sanitized rich HTML in `messages.body`; every preview in the app (sidebar rows, notifications, reply quotes) MUST route through `lib/messageText.ts` so only the bubble itself renders HTML. Shipped and working: rich-text composer (TipTap), threads (`parent_message_id` self-FK), edits (`edited` flag), reactions (inline `reactions_json`), per-message bookmarks, pin/unpin, 'delete for me' (`message_deletions` side table) and 'delete for everyone' (tombstone via `messages.deleted`), forwarding with `forward_count`, scheduled messages (compose-now/deliver-later via a backend poller and `scheduled_messages`), keyset-paginated history (`?before&limit<=100`), WhatsApp-style reciprocal read receipts, voice notes (`type='voice'`), and a FULLTEXT search index (`idx_messages_fts`, BOOLEAN mode). Realtime delivery is the single `MESSAGE_NEW` room echo, which doubles as the send-ack (the optimistic render reconciles against it).
18.1.4 Calls and meetings — verified application logic

Both 1:1/group calls (driven inside CoLabV1) and scheduled meetings (driven by MeetingStage) are built on LiveKit and share one CSS source (`.ms-*` classes). Verified application behavior includes: server-side LiveKit token minting gated by membership (an IDOR guard on `call_<id>`, conversation-member checks on `conv_<id>`, and `meetingService.enterRoom` enforcing eject→lock→lobby on `meeting_<id>`); 1:1→group promotion; group host controls (mute-all, per-participant mute, remove) gated to owner/admin; full meeting host/co-host controls (lobby admit/deny/admit-all, lock, eject that persists across token re-mint via `meeting_ejected`, promote/demote/readmit); persisted in-meeting chat (`meeting_messages`, last 100 replayed on join), hand-raise and reactions over Redis-backed `huddleStore`; join-by-meeting-ID/link (the meeting UUID *is* the access credential); structured Outlook-style recurrence (`recurrence_rule`, migration 0047); call-lifecycle system pills in chat; voicemail; and device hot-swap mid-call. A WebRTC diagnostics layer (`callDiagnostics.ts` + `CallDebugPanel.tsx`) polls `getStats()` and emits grep-able `[CALLDIAG]` traces distinguishing 'TURN advertised but not reachable' from 'no TURN advertised'.

text: 18.2.1 E2EE Phase 1 — exact scope and honest limits

CoLab ships a real but deliberately conservative end-to-end-encryption implementation, and it is important not to overclaim it. **Plain language:** when turned on, direct messages between two people are scrambled on the sender's device and can only be unscrambled on the recipient's devices — the server stores only opaque ciphertext and public keys and cannot read the content. **Engineering:** it is custom native Web Crypto ECIES (P-256 ECDH + HKDF-SHA-256 + AES-GCM-256), NOT the Signal protocol despite the `SignalStore.ts` filename. The long-term device key is a non-extractable P-256 CryptoKey in IndexedDB; each message uses a fresh ephemeral keypair per recipient device; AES-GCM AAD binds version|sender|recipient|conversationId|nonce so the server cannot splice or replay envelopes. One sealed envelope is produced per recipient device plus the sender's own other devices.

title: E2EE — do not overclaim
text: Scope is DM and self-conversations ONLY. Groups, channels, calls and meetings are plaintext (LiveKit SFU media is not E2EE; distributeGroupSenderKey is a no-op placeholder). There is NO forward secrecy yet — per-message ephemerals protect against the server but not against theft of a device's long-term key (a ratchet is Phase 2). The 100 one-time prekeys generated per device are DORMANT in v1 (reserved for a future X3DH/Double-Ratchet). The safety-number is implemented in lib/e2ee/safety.ts but verified-by-grep to be referenced ONLY inside the e2ee lib — it is wired into NO UI component, so safety-number verification is genuinely pending. The whole feature is OFF by default and fail-closed when on (it throws rather than ever silently sending plaintext on an E2EE conversation).
18.2.2 Recording — two paths, one not provisioned

Recording is PARTIAL because the backend is complete but one of its two paths depends on infrastructure that is off. Path (a) is **server-side LiveKit Egress**: gated by `EGRESS_ENABLED` and an egress worker container; when that container is not running the API returns an honest 503 rather than failing silently. Path (b) is **client-side MediaRecorder** (`uploadClientRecording`): it works without egress, stores the webm/mp4 to S3/MinIO, and plays back through the auth-gated, membership-checked `/api/meetings/:id/recordings/:rid/download` stream. In current deployments only path (b) is functional because the egress container is not provisioned.
18.2.3 Accessibility and brand-token contrast

The design system ships an extensive accessibility toolkit — high-contrast variants (`body.dark.high-contrast`, `body.oled.high-contrast`), reduce-motion, larger-text, dyslexia-font, blur-media, density modes and a six-theme palette — all toggled via body classes in `applySettings()`. This is real and works. The incomplete part is **brand-token contrast**: the default indigo accent (`--ac #5e6ad2`) and some derived token combinations do not universally meet WCAG AA contrast on every surface/theme pairing without the high-contrast toggle. This is tracked in the Technical Debt subsection rather than claimed as fully solved.

text: 18.3.1 Agents and MCP — reserved, not running

Both the `agents/` and `mcp/` modules participate in the monorepo build/lint graph (they are npm workspaces, linted by depcruise/madge) but ship no runtime behavior in the product. The repository's own `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` labels them as scaffolds, and the in-app `AgentsView.tsx` is a static governance/marketing page that renders 'No agents connected' / 'No MCP server is configured in this deployment'. The MCP server is more built than the agents module — it has 20 real tool definitions and a working stdio JSON-RPC loop that proxies to the REST backend — but it has no `initialize` handshake, its SSE transport is discovery-only (cannot invoke tools), it is not containerized, and nothing in the product invokes it. The working in-product AI (the `Agen-X` summarize/ask in `aiService.ts`) is a completely separate implementation that does not use the `agents/` module despite a coincidental shared method name.

title: Do not confuse the three AI surfaces
text: (1) aiService.ts — the REAL, working OpenAI-compatible summarize/ask backend (off when LLM_BASE_URL unset). (2) agents/ — an empty scaffold whose methods throw. (3) mcp/ — a standalone REST-proxy prototype not wired into any deployment. Only (1) does real work, and even (1) is mostly hidden behind feature flags / has no ask UI.
18.4 Technical Debt

This is the accumulated debt that a future maintainer will pay interest on. None of it is a bug today, but each item raises the cost of change or the risk of regression, and each should be on the long-term roadmap.
18.4.1 The CoLabV1 god-component and re-render pattern

`CoLabV1.tsx` is ~9,039 lines and owns nearly all application state — `mode`, theme, conversations, active conversation, settings, modals, toasts, call state, plus several inline views (Activity ~line 5003, Dashboard ~line 5477). State is plain React `useState` with no Redux/Zustand/Jotai and effectively no app-level Context; props are drilled into child views. The mitigation already in place is a set of `useRef` mirrors (`tokenRef`, `messagesByConvRef`, `socketRef`, `settingsRef`, `meRef`, `usersRef`, `conversationsRef`) so callbacks read latest state without unstable dependencies, frozen `EMPTY_ARR`/`EMPTY_OBJ` constants for stable identities, and `React.memo` on heavy children (ChatView). **Debt:** because the god-component holds the socket-event sinks, a naive change can reintroduce a full-tree re-render on every socket event. The proven pattern for further work is memoized shells (ChatView/Rail) fed stable props via refs — but the structural debt of a 9k-line single component remains, and ChatView itself is ~6,296 lines.

text: 18.4.2 Brand-token contrast debt

The default accent and a number of status/surface token combinations were chosen for brand look first; not all of them clear WCAG AA contrast on every theme without the high-contrast toggle. This is a design-token debt: it should be paid by re-deriving accent-on-surface tokens per theme so that contrast is correct by default, rather than relying on the user to enable high-contrast mode. It is enumerated in the enterprise UI audit work referenced in the design-system section of this handbook.
18.4.3 Dependency and supply-chain advisories

The repository carries security tooling config (`audit-ci.json`, `.dependency-cruiser.cjs`, `knip.json`, `.secretlintrc.json`). Transitive dependency advisories surface periodically through the deep React/Next/LiveKit/AWS-SDK dependency trees; these are largely transitive (not direct) and should be triaged on a schedule via `npm audit` / audit-ci rather than chased reactively. The native E2EE path deliberately avoids adding a heavy crypto dependency (it uses built-in Web Crypto), and `@signalapp/libsignal-client` is aliased OUT of the client bundle precisely so a native Rust NAPI dependency never ships to the browser — a deliberate debt-avoidance choice worth preserving.
18.4.4 Other tracked debt

text: 18.5.1 Troubleshooting the most common one: calls fail on a new deployment

By far the most frequent operational issue is 'calls don't work after we deployed'. It is almost never application code. The diagnostic order is: (1) confirm the page is served over HTTPS — a non-secure context silently blocks `getUserMedia`; (2) confirm the LiveKit signalling URL is being derived from the request origin (`wss://<host>/livekit`) and is not a stale `ws://localhost`; (3) confirm the SFU media ports are reachable from the client network (7532/udp, 7531/tcp); (4) confirm a TURN relay is advertised AND reachable (the `[CALLDIAG]` trace distinguishes 'advertised but not reachable — check 3478/5349/443' from 'no TURN advertised'); (5) if signalling is healthy but media fails, it is the ICE/DTLS media plane (TURN/firewall/region), not the `/livekit` proxy.

text: 18.6 Production Risks
These are the risks that can cause user-visible failure or a security exposure in production. Each is grounded in the real deployment configuration, and each has a concrete mitigation.
18.6.1 Cross-network media depends on TURN, firewall and region

**Risk.** Calls and meetings work perfectly on a LAN or VPN but can silently fail to deliver media when the two endpoints are on different networks (office Wi-Fi to home 4G, hotel/corporate NAT, etc.). The signalling plane stays healthy, so the app looks connected while no audio/video flows. **Cause.** Media is WebRTC ICE/DTLS over UDP/TCP and, for locked-down NATs, must fall back to a TURN relay; if the SFU media ports or the coturn relay are not reachable across the remote network, the candidate-pair never completes. **Mitigation.** Provision and verify a reachable TURN relay (coturn supports turns: over 443 — the only transport that reliably traverses locked-down mobile/corporate/hotel NAT), open the SFU media ports at the firewall, and use the `[CALLDIAG]` observability to confirm a relay candidate pair is selected. This is an infrastructure responsibility, not an app fix.
18.6.2 Single-region SFU latency

**Risk.** A LiveKit SFU is not peer-to-peer — every participant's media goes client→SFU→client. A single SFU in us-east means India-based users see ~200–300 ms RTT even in the same room, degrading call quality. **Mitigation (designed, not deployed).** `docker-compose.mumbai.yml` + `docs/DEPLOY_MUMBAI_REGION.md` relocate ONLY the media engine (SFU + coturn + a LiveKit-state Redis) to asia-south1 (~20–40 ms) with no application code change — signalling continues to flow through the existing nginx `/livekit` proxy, media goes direct to the regional box. Until that is provisioned, distant-user latency is an accepted risk.
18.6.3 Secrets shipped in deployment artifacts

title: Secrets travel in the deploy zip and committed config
text: scripts/package-deploy-live.ps1 builds a CoLab-LIVE-deploy zip that ships FILLED .env.live / .env.teams / .env.local plus a database/dumps SQL snapshot. A real static coturn TURN password is hardcoded in the committed infrastructure/coturn/turnserver.conf and in deploy docs. Default MinIO root creds (colabminio/colabminio123 or colab/colab) are weak and unenforced. Treat every deploy artifact as secret-bearing: restrict who can receive the zip, rotate the TURN credential and MinIO creds, and never commit a real .env. The production boot guard refuses to start with bundled default AUTH_JWT_SECRET / LIVEKIT_API_SECRET, which is the backstop — but it does NOT cover the TURN or MinIO secrets.
18.6.4 Storage, encryption-at-rest and the silent fallback

items: No encryption at rest by default — MinIO server-side encryption is not configured; objects sit plain on the volume unless app-level E2EE is on (off by default).
Internal backend→MinIO hop is plain http://minio:9000; external client transit security depends entirely on the deployment TLS front.
Silent DB-blob fallback — if MinIO is unreachable, uploads quietly land in MySQL with no alert. Monitor MinIO health explicitly.
Presigned-URL feature is wired but bypassed by the same-origin proxy delivery model, so it is not a production attack surface today.

text: 18.6.5 Data-loss and rollback discipline

**Risk.** `docker compose down -v` deletes the `colab_mysqldata` volume — total data loss. **Mitigation.** Migrations are additive/idempotent and tracked in `schema_migrations` with a statement-level idempotent runner that resumes from a failure point (no crash-loop), and the named volume persists across rebuilds; but the operational rule is firm: always `mysqldump` before any deploy, use `down` (never `down -v`), and rely on `migrate-local-to-prod.sh` taking a prod backup first as its own rollback. The live `collab.resulticks.com` deployment writes to its OWN bundled MySQL container volume by default — back THAT up, not the empty corporate DB.
18.6.6 Single-instance assumptions

The HTTP rate limiter and several ephemeral call structures are per-process in-memory. The system is correct on a single backend instance; running multiple instances behind a load balancer requires the Redis adapter (already supported and gated by `REDIS_URL`, with a 3 s readiness race and in-memory fallback) and would expose the per-instance rate-limit and ephemeral-state gaps. Plan for Redis-backed shared state before horizontal scale-out.

title: The honest one-sentence status
text: CoLab is a fully working, enterprise-styled collaboration product across messaging, calls, meetings, tasks, reminders, files and notifications — with AI, agents, MCP, multi-region media and Signal-grade E2EE deliberately fenced off as flagged-off, scaffolded, or Phase-2 work, and with cross-network calling resting on correct TURN/firewall/region infrastructure rather than on application code.
